#6662. This Golden-Hour Honolulu Wedding Shared the Same View as the Couple’s First Date

A tropical storm warning couldn’t stop Mele Hamasaki and Daniel Croix Henderson from going on their first date. “I think we both had a special feeling about each other and were just way too excited to postpone,” Mele says of their May 6, 2021 meeting. “The connection was instantaneous and life-altering.” Sitting at Tantalus Lookout in Honolulu, the two discussed nature, their creative processes, and more. “As we both had hoped, the storm never came,” says Mele. “Instead, we were blessed with a stunning sunset and an empty park entirely for us!”

“All these years later, I look at the life we’ve built together—our individual and shared dreams coming into focus, the films we’ve co-created, the communities we’ve rooted in, and the curiosity we still bring to one another—and realize our first date was a microcosm of everything that followed,” adds Daniel, an actor and filmmaker.

On New Year's Day in 2025, Mele and Daniel returned to that very same spot to watch the sunset over a picnic. Daniel had an engagement ring on hand, ready to propose. “I kept checking my pocket over and over again on the day for the ring, realizing I’d never held an object so precious to me,” he remembers. “I’ll never forget the moment when she said ‘yes!’ Tears welled up in our eyes and I felt like I’d entered a portal.” Says Mele, “At that point, I knew I was going to spend the rest of my life with Daniel but I’ve always found the ritual and ceremony of making a life-long commitment to a person and their family really profound and courageous.” When they returned to their home, Daniel coordinated with Mele’s mom and aunts to have the space adorned with flowers and vines from her “Popo’s” house. Adds Mele, “Always the romantic, this guy!”

When the bride and groom chose where to tie the knot, they decided to maintain the same view as when they first met. A friend’s family offered their historic Honolulu home, which provided a dramatic backdrop of the city and ocean. “We live in town and have the most pilina (connection) as a couple to the ridges and waters of Honolulu,” explains Mele, who grew up on Oʻahu. “So having the wedding on the south side of the island was very important to us. Our intention for having it on the peak of the Lion’s Gate Portal was to fill the world with as much aloha as we could!” Notes Daniel, “Our friend’s family opening their home to our wedding was an act of kindness and generosity that we’ll always remember.”

As a designer and producer in her day-to-day life, Mele put her skills to work when planning the wedding. “As soon as we reframed wedding planning as pre-production, everything locked into place for us,” she says. “We hired ‘department heads,’ scheduled fittings and rehearsals, managed the budget, and sent out call sheets to our guests. I used my design skills to collage and mock up everything I could think of to ensure details were visualized!” The bride also partnered with wedding planner Karisa Ramolete Hayashi of Say I Do By Karisa to direct the show. “Karisa grew up right down the street from the venue, which felt very aligned,” says the bride. “It was important for us to work with someone who was connected to Hawaiʻi in the same way we are.”

The couple also called on their community to bring their celebration to life. “I was so moved by how many friends contributed their creative gifts and energy toward preparation,” reflects the groom. “Our family members and friends from my bachelor party came to the house before the wedding several times to help prepare. It took an island of love, creativity, and generosity to bring this all together.”

That community also guided the couple as they sought out their wardrobes for the weekend. The bride kicked off the wedding weekend in an ivory look by Hawaiian designer Rocket Ahuna. She first connected with the designer when attending his debut show on the island. “He ended up designing an entire capsule wardrobe for me which I got to wear on my bachelorette in Kauaʻi and throughout the wedding weekend!” Mele says.

Mele admits she struggled to find a ceremony dress for a full year and almost wore a vintage dress she didn’t truly love. “Luckily, my very bossy cousin Aja Dang demanded I keep trying and reminded me that I should never settle,” says Mele. “My instinct told me to check out Loho Bride in West Hollywood one more time before it was too late. Aja and my friend Helix came with me and encouraged me to try on the Calico Grace Gown from Bon Bride.” The gown featured raw stitching details, a bleached calico fabric—“perfect for the humidity of Honolulu summers”—and draping that lent a sexier touch to the shape. “This was the first dress that finally felt truly me,” the bride says.

To accessorize, Mele paired the dress with a pleated handkerchief veil from Danielle Frankel, “which brought the whole look together and made me feel like an ethereal queen!” The bride’s friend Karen of Jos Mundo gifted her a custom pair of bridal shoes that were a take on the brand’s Marikina Mule. “It was so fun to go through the design process with her,” Mele remembers. “It was the first time she had her team emboss initials inside the shoe—a customization they will now be offering to all brides!” As for beauty, Mele worked with Risa Hoshino for makeup, and Jonah Dela-Cruz to craft two hair looks for the night. She says, “He understood the assignment!”

Daniel knew he “had to look sharp” for his wedding day. “I wanted to wear something with enough formality to honor the moment, while also having a free-flowing, playful, and creative twist that felt danceable and like myself,” he says. The groom looked back through family photos for inspiration as well. “My stylist Henna Koskinen and I spoke a lot about these influences, and when I tried on the Dries Van Noten suit, I felt a special energy—and everything felt right,” he says. He paired his suit with a textured Cult Gaia shirt and Saint Laurent loafers.

For his second look, Daniel worked with Isabel Sicat, designer of Toqa, to create an ensemble filled with small talismans that connected him with the ocean. “Isabel’s team did extraordinary work—every shell, bead, and charm was hand-sewn into the raw silk shantung dyed tuxedo-inspired trouser and tailcoat-like shirt,” he explains. “The cowrie shell adornment was of particular significance to me—an amulet of protection which connects generations of my ancestors. Found in West Africa and along the coasts of Georgia and the Carolinas, [it’s] known as a symbol of prosperity, protection, and power.”

When Mele’s original plan for a second look fell through, Sicat was able to craft her a complementary look to wear as she danced the hula later in the evening. “Without hesitation, she immediately stepped up to the plate and hustled to create a custom heat-treated top and pleated wrap skirt that perfectly matched Daniel’s look,” says Mele. “It was a dream to wear.”

The wedding weekend kicked off with a welcome picnic in Kapiʻolani Park. Mele and Daniel produced a public art show in the same spot with artist Noe Tanigawa a year before that commemorated the 80th anniversary of the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. “Reflecting on this project one year later reminded us of the delicacy of peace and our responsibility to live in harmony with the natural world, with our relationships, and with ourselves,” she says. The welcome event was full of connection and crafts. “At each table we had a setup to make lei with string and needle, which nourished the many days ahead—adorning our ancestral altar and decorating a lot of the areas of the wedding,” shares Daniel. “Shoutout to Karisa’s aunty for the pounds of puakenikeni and crown flower from her yard!”

The next day, the couple came together with their friends and family at their ceremony overlooking Honolulu. Mele’s mom officiated, Daniel’s mom shared a passage, and their fathers served as ring bearers and also performed a water unity ceremony. “When we were up there between the Lion’s Gate Portal and pillars Ren of Renko Floral designed, it felt otherworldly but also very quotidian—like it was just us, holding hands in the park like we always do,” says Mele. Daniel remembers the entire ceremony as deeply moving and memorable. He shares that he felt, “Elated, floating, vibing, teary, hyperpresent—witnessing Mele in these moments was truly the most beautiful sight, and holding hands with her through it all was deeply grounding.” The newlyweds remember being filled with joy (and a bit of surprise at impact) as their loved ones showered rice over them.

The rest of the evening was filled with connection, happiness, and plenty of music. After speeches, the bride’s father recited a poem as the groom’s father played bass, Hawaiian music legend Brother Noland played his hits, the bride danced hula, and the groom sang “Knocks Me Off My Feet" with their band Hawaiian Soul. “What felt the most special was watching Mele dance hula,” says Daniel. “She danced as a kid but stepped away from it for over a decade, and only recently returned to the practice. It was special to witness her magic and talent in this way, and I’ll never forget her glow!” Says Mele, “It was a total portal of love, high vibration, and celebration!”

The after-party was held indoors in a space transformed by artist Bradley Capello into a “pink jewel box” filled with mirrors, disco balls, and a large Pegge Hopper cutout. “Dancing the night away on the lauhala mats that my mom and her lauhala friends wove and resting on the Tutuvi pillows they sewed was a truly magical experience,” shares Mele. “You could feel the aloha through your feet and tush!” A low-key beach day followed, giving friends and family time to say goodbye. “Soaking in salt water was the perfect way to process everything,” says Daniel.

Both the bride and groom share that they don’t take their wedding or their love for granted. “I think celebrating love and choosing love is a superpower,” says Mele.

Nothing beats soaking in golden hour next to your handsome fiancé in a Rocket Ahuna set and Jos Mundo shoes the night before your wedding! —Mele

Kapiʻolani Beach Park, Kaimana Beach Hotel, and Kāpua Channel are special places that have connected us and our community over the years. We used them as our home base throughout the wedding weekend. —Mele

We had all our guests string lei during our welcome picnic. Shoutout to our wedding planner Karisa Ramolete Hayashi’s aunt for the pounds of puakenikeni and crown flower she harvested from her yard! The lei traveled with us—from adorning our ancestral altar at the wedding to surrounding our condo with flowers after the festivities to landing in its final home in the forest in Makiki after our honeymoon. —Daniel

This wedding felt like such a transformational rite of passage and a dream come true, so of course I had to look sharp! I chose a Dries Van Noten suit and Cult Gaia shirt, tied together with Saint Laurent loafers. Styled by Henna Koskinen. —Daniel

The anticipation of seeing my beautiful bride was so intense. My jitters faded when my best man joined me and helped me get ready. —Daniel

My best man and best friend, Max Mooney. From meeting at camp when we were 15 years old to being college roommates dreaming of making films together to bringing those dreams into reality today in our adult lives, he’s been a pillar in my life for over 15 years, and I’m so grateful he was there for this very special day. —Daniel

My mom and beloved friend Iris making sure I look presentable for my big day! —Mele

After struggling to find a dress for months, I found the Calico Grace Gown from Bon Bride at Loho Bride. This was the first dress that finally felt like me. I fell in love with the raw stitching, the unbleached cotton calico, and the hitch detail on the side! —Mele

A moment for my beautiful bouquet by Renko Floral—a magical arrangement of kaunaʻoa, ʻilima, and orchids!

This pleated Danielle Frankel veil put the whole look together and truly made me feel like an ethereal queen. —Mele

Can’t believe I get to see those dimples for the rest of my life! —Mele

The first look… I have no words for the intense rush of this extremely beautiful moment! Mele looked absolutely gorgeous. —Daniel

My mom has always encouraged me to follow my heart. Her joy in this moment meant so much to me. —Daniel

Crying and cheering on my sweet Dad, who has been there for me through it all! —Mele

My beautiful, powerful mama. I was moments away from turning into a puddle when she gave me her strength, as she always does! —Mele

Our dear friend Reise Kochi sourced pōhuehue and found shrubs from the property to create the most enchanting hanging florals. Artist Erin Nagamine hand painted our welcome sign.

As guests arrived for the wedding ceremony, I kept thinking of all the people who poured their love into this day. I felt so humbled. It took so many people to bring it all together and celebrate this love! —Daniel

Our chefs Jason and Grace of Pidgin Food Co. welcomed our guests with seasonal fruit covered in their signature chamui. So ono (delicious)!

Looking out at the same ocean and cityscape we saw the first day we met felt especially meaningful. This time with both craters, Lēʻahi (Diamond Head) and Pūowaina (Punchbowl) in the horizon! —Daniel

Renko Floral used deciduous plumeria branches sculpted into asymmetrical forms grounded by bananas and draped in dendrobium lei! The perfect portal for our Lion’s Gate Portal ceremony! —Mele

My siblings, Enzo, Caitlin, and K. sang a beautiful rendition of the St. Francis Prayer, “Make me a channel of your peace,” as I walked down the aisle with my parents. My mom sang this to us when we were kids. So sweet! —Daniel

Having strings during our ceremony was a non-negotiable for Daniel! —Mele

Walking down the aisle with my parents, and seeing so many people I love—many who flew in from all over the world—was so joyful and moving. I felt such a rush of intense emotion as I took this walk, and it was made all the more special to share this moment with my parents. —Daniel

My dad has been by my side for every important moment of my life. I love and cherish him and look up to his example: always patient, creative, and grounded. —Daniel

It was so meaningful to have my friends’ daughters and Daniel’s little cousin as our flower girls! They all did an excellent job. High five! —Mele

Cherishing this moment forever and ever. —Mele

Highly recommend finding a life partner who looks at you like this! —Mele

Watching Mele walk down the aisle with her parents brought me to a euphoric high. It looked as if the sun was shining from her heart, and no one could take their eyes off of her! —Daniel

Can you tell we love each other yet? —Mele

Have you ever seen a more radiant bride? I mean come on! —Daniel

Emily and Ezra basking in love! We love love! —Mele

Our fathers, Richard and Edgar, were our ring bearers and helped us perform a water unity ceremony. My dad Edgar brought water from the Buffalo River, near where I grew up. Mele’s parents brought ‘Āpuakea rain from Kāne’ohe—the rain she is named after and grew up with. —Daniel

We poured the unified water into the earth to remember and honor our ancestors, and the journeys they’ve taken for us to stand here together. —Mele

We were fortunate to have the most elegant officiant, my mom Jennifer. Adorned with the most stunning lei of pikake and ilima made by the one and only, Island Boy. —Mele

The elements were with us during our vows. When we spoke of wind, we felt the wind. When we spoke of rain, we felt a sprinkle of rain. When we were closing out our vows, the sun came out in full force to shine down on us. Mahalo e nā akua! —Mele

Our very first kiss as husband and wife. —Daniel

We had everyone throw rice to shower blessings and abundance upon us. The rice was harder than we expected, but it was so much fun. —Daniel

I never thought I’d enjoy being pelted in the face with rice, but it truly did mark a passage of a new beginning in such a joyful and present way! —Mele

Hugging my grandfather Bernard right after the ceremony. He spent his life and career as a musician and a woodworker restoring precious furniture. I’ve always admired his creative streak and hope to carry it on! —Daniel

Another Renko Floral arrangement to melt your mind! —Mele

This was Chef Jason and Chef Grace of Pigin Food Co’s very first catering job. The creativity, life force energy, and aloha they poured into our custom menu were heroic. We can’t wait to see where this journey takes them. —Daniel

Our sweet friends, Stefi and Karam, welcoming us into the married club! —Mele

How can you not smile at everyone’s smiles?!

Our first moments together as a married couple soaking in the view.

Introducing Mr. and Mrs. Daniel Croix Henderson and Mele Hamasaki!

We gifted Bodha incense and Small Kine Gift lighters to all our guests. I call it “incense-on-the-go” for those emergency moments when you just need to light some incense. —Mele

Our extraordinary friend Kano Watanabe poured her heart into the handmade wauke paper for our printed menus, which our incredible friend Kera Rasavanh meticulously screenprinted. Framing these menus because they are truly a work of art! —Mele

Our first dance was to “Lovers Rock” by Sade, which our beloved friend Oona Roche sang and our talented friends Pei-Ling Kao and Gigi Axelrode choreographed. —Mele

When we first met, we read a book called “Dancing the Dream” and we’ve been doing just that ever since. —Daniel

Another rite of passage as husband and wife—eating cake! —Mele

Iris giving a beautiful speech about her bestie Mele. —Daniel

Most definitely laughing at Daniel’s best man Max’s speech. —Mele

We had some rain pass through which meant parasols up! —Mele

Allyson Burgess, ever the crafty one, turns the table cloth and napkin into a look. —Mele

The dads, Richard and Edgar, performed an original poem and jazz fusion piece and introduced themselves as “THE TWO DADS!” It was very punk rock, and we are patiently awaiting the album... —Daniel

The legendary Brother Noland sings “Coconut Girl!” An iconic, core memory that will live in our bodies, minds, and souls forever. —Mele

Jasai Chase-Owens, William E. Rouse, and Robyn Rouse: unbothered by the rain and entranced by the performances. —Daniel

It was such a heart-melty dream to watch Mele dance with her hula sisters, Gigi and Kalani Axelrode. —Daniel

My talented friend Isabel Sicat of Toqa handcrafted a custom heat-treated top and a pleated wrap skirt for me to dance in. She made me feel luminous on the dance floor! —Mele

I began dancing with Kumu Hula Māpuana de Silva of Hālau Mohala ‘Ilima when I was four years old. After years away, I found my way back last year. Being able to perform for Daniel and our family and friends was an incredibly meaningful and special moment for me. —Mele

Daniel knocked me off my feet singing Stevie Wonder’s “Knocks Me Off My Feet” with the sensational band, Hawaiian Soul. —Mele

The pass of rain made everything feel more and more magical. —Daniel

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6660. "11/10" Tuna Melt and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6659. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6658. The Deeper Meaning Behind Kate Middleton’s Remembrance Day Earrings

Kate Middleton’s jewelry choices often carry a significance beyond their sparkle. Across this year’s Remembrance commemorations, the Princess of Wales paid subtle tributes to two of the most significant women in the royal family’s history: Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana. And the personal stories behind her chosen earrings offered a poignant reminder of how royal jewels are passed between generations.

On Sunday morning, Kate joined senior members of the royal family for the National Service of Remembrance at London’s Cenotaph, where King Charles III and Prince William laid wreaths in honor of those who have lost their lives in military service. Watching from a balcony alongside Queen Camilla, the Princess wore a sharply tailored black Catherine Walker coat (a new addition to her wardrobe, from a long-favored designer that Diana also loved), with a double-breasted silhouette, velvet buttons, and a high velvet collar, topped with an asymmetric wide-brimmed hat by Jane Taylor. But it was the familiar pearl-and-diamond earrings that carried a particularly personal significance.

The Collingwood Pearl and Diamond Drop Earrings once belonged to her late mother-in-law, Princess Diana. Given to Diana by London jewelers Collingwood ahead of her wedding to the then-Prince Charles in 1981, the earrings feature diamond-studded settings from which large, lustrous pearls are suspended. They became a mainstay of Diana's jewelry collection, accompanying her to glittering state banquets and royal engagements. In the years since, Kate has made the heirlooms part of her own wardrobe, continuing their story as the current Princess of Wales and wearing them on multiple royal engagements.

There was further symbolism in Sunday’s accessories. Kate fastened three red poppies to her coat alongside the HMS Glasgow Brooch, a sterling silver piece specially commissioned by Glasgow jeweler James Porter & Son in 2025 to mark her role as sponsor of the Royal Navy warship. Its design incorporates the ship’s crest, the Scottish thistle, and a depiction of St. Kentigern, Glasgow's patron saint. The three poppies, have been linked to Kate’s own family history: three brothers of her great-grandmother Olive were killed during the First World War, although the Princess has never publicly confirmed the connection.

The previous evening, Kate had reached for a different pair of royal heirlooms. Attending the Royal British Legion’s Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall with Prince William, she wore Queen Elizabeth II’s Diamond Orbital Pendant Earrings, also known as the Queen’s Diamond Frame Earrings. The intricate jewels feature a floral diamond cluster at the ear and a cascade of graduating diamonds enclosed within a glittering frame. While their precise origins remain unknown, Elizabeth wore them on several occasions, including the State Opening of Parliament in 2012.

Kate Middleton first wore the earrings publicly in 2016 and has since chosen them for significant moments, including Princess Eugenie’s wedding in 2018 and her own official 40th birthday portraits in 2022. For Saturday’s ceremony, she paired them with a black-and-white pleated polka-dot dress by Alessandra Rich—another sentimental wardrobe repeat, having previously worn it to Prince Philip’s memorial service at Westminster Abbey in March 2022. A black suede Ba&Sh belt, pointed Alessandra Rich slingbacks, a velvet Jimmy Choo clutch, and her Irish Guards Regimental Brooch finished the ensemble.

Across two consecutive days, the Princess’s choices traced a line through three generations of royal women. From Elizabeth’s glittering diamonds to Diana’s unmistakable pearls, these were jewels carrying memories as well as history. And at a time of national reflection, Kate’s wardrobe offered its own quiet tribute to those who came before her.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. #6654. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6653. A Visit With Six Women Farmers Across the Americas

Women make up nearly half of the agricultural workforce in developing countries, yet they account for fewer than one in five of the world’s agricultural landholders. As rising food prices, climate volatility, and food security concerns put farming back at the center of public debate, the United Nations designated 2026 as the International Year of the Woman Farmer, bringing renewed attention to a workforce that remains central to food systems while often excluded from land ownership, financing, and decision-making.

Between January and August 2026, I spent two weeks living with each of six women farmers. In the Galápagos, María Espinoza grows food without chemicals on islands that still import most of what they eat. In Guatemala, Aurelia Beb Tec cultivates cacao on land returned to her Q’eqchi’ community through a reparations process after decades of dispossession and war. In Chiapas, Yumara Salas Ramírez became the first woman to serve as secretary of her coffee cooperative. In Haiti, Lucianie Vil, a 70-year-old Madan Sara, carries her harvest by mule to the border market of Anse-à-Pitre. In Arkansas, Samantha Noble coordinates poultry production at a ranch devoted to regenerative farming. And in Honduras, Milexy Rodríguez lost 15 cows in 40 days when drought dried up her lagoon, rebuilding by drilling a well and diversifying.

The resulting photographs follow the rhythm of their days and the pressures shaping food production where they live. They also show what these women have built: cooperatives, savings groups, a coffee brand of their own, knowledge passed on to their daughters and neighbors.

María Espinoza, 54, lives in the highlands of San Cristóbal Island, in the Galápagos. She is up at 5 a.m. to feed her animals before heading into the fields, where she grows fruit and vegetables on a plot she slowly reclaimed from invasive blackberry. She lives alone but the farm sets the rhythm of her day, keeps her company, and puts food on the table.

Fresh water on the island is scarce and depends on El Junco lagoon, while pests and food shipped in from the mainland make farming hard. María uses no chemicals, makes her own organic fertilizers, and, since 2023, has trained in protecting soil and crops without pesticides.

María Espinoza gets dressed in her bedroom before heading out to work on her farm.

Espinoza pushes a wheelbarrow loaded with freshly harvested produce. Back home, she will wash and prepare it to take to market the next day.

Espinoza tends her stall at the agroecological market organized by Heifer, where she sells her produce alongside other farmers every Wednesday.

Yumara Salas Ramírez, 30, lives in Santa Rita, a community in the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, among coffee farms and dense forest at the edge of the El Triunfo Biosphere Reserve. A single mother to her daughter Ximena, she works at the Sierra Azul Cooperative’s collection center, where she checks coffee quality and is learning to cup. She was the first woman to serve as the cooperative’s secretary and is part of Café 89, the coffee brand of the cooperative’s women producers, created to make their work visible. Chiapas grows 41% of Mexico’s coffee, yet women hold only about a quarter of Mexico’s ejido land rights. Yumara speaks openly about the machismo that still holds women back, and about a region hit by drug-trafficking violence, climate change, and pests such as the coffee berry borer. Still, she chose to stay.

Yumara Salas Ramírez picks coffee during the harvest on the hillsides of Santa Rita, Chiapas.

Salas Ramírez rakes the coffee at the processing mill to ensure it dries evenly.

Salas Ramírez and Anayanci Domínguez Vazquez smell the cups during a cupping session at the Sierra Azul Cooperative.

Aurelia Beb Tec, 44, grows cacao on five manzanas (about eight and a half acres) in Pinares, a Maya Q’eqchi’ village in Alta Verapaz. Every Wednesday she walks the slopes with her daughters Brenda, Mayra, and Mirna, picking the ripe pods and selling the harvest to the local association. She planted every tree herself. At home she roasts the beans on a clay comal, grinds them on stone, and makes hot chocolate, while her daughters learn to make bars with cardamom and milk.

For decades the Q’eqchi’ of Pinares were dispossessed by landowners and forced into servitude; then came repression and civil war. After the peace accords, a reparations program brought land, seeds, and support, and cacao proved the best crop. In 2014 the community founded APIDIP (Asociación del Pueblo Indígena para el Desarrollo Integral Productivo de la Aldea Pinares), which today has 156 members and exports fair trade, organic cacao.

Aurelia Beb Tec walks among the cacao trees in the rain, searching for ripe pods during the harvest.

Beb Tec and her daughter Brenda sort cacao in their kitchen.

Lucianie Vil, 70, is a Madan Sara, one of the women traders who travel Haiti’s roads and markets to support their families and feed their communities. She lives in Ma Rouge, a scattered village in the mountains of southeastern Haiti. Every Wednesday she walks up to her plot in Thiotte, where she harvests pineapples, oranges, passion fruit, and coffee with her husband and grandchildren, then carries her harvest down the mountain by mule and sells it at the border market of Anse-à-Pitre on Fridays. More than half of Haiti’s population now faces food insecurity, and rural trade depends on routes increasingly cut off by violence and on harvests threatened by drought. Lucianie started selling at 13 and raised seven children on what the land gave her. Like the bird the Madan Sara are named after, she never stops moving.

On a narrow mountain trail, Lucianie Vil walks ahead of a mule loaded with fruit and vegetables on the three- hour journey from Romain to her home in Ma Rouge.

Vil clears a path with her machete through the undergrowth on her plot in Romain.

Vil counts the day’s earnings with a fellow vendor at the market in Anse-à-Pitre. She reports that a day at the market brings in around $150 in sales, of which she keeps roughly $100 once transport and other costs are paid.

Before dawn at Heifer Ranch, Samantha Noble already has her boots on. She checks the mobile chicken coops, looks over the birds, and plans with her team which paddock to move that day. Born in Minnesota in 1993, she grew up around animals and ended up studying animal science.

A professor told her about Heifer International and she came to the ranch as a volunteer, first guiding school visits, then rotating among livestock species. Poultry has been her trade ever since, and today she is the ranch’s poultry production coordinator. Heifer Ranch, about 40 miles west of Little Rock, is a living laboratory for regenerative livestock farming, where planned grazing, holistic management, and animal health are researched and demonstrated. Her goal is to help other producers save time, improve their farms, and find a better balance between work and life.

Morning fog over the ranch roads in Perryville, Arkansas.

Noble, the ranch’s poultry production coordinator, walks through one of the mobile coops built on the pasture.

Noble takes two of her children to a swimming lesson.

Milexy Rodríguez, 46, lives in El Nance, a rural community in Olanchito, in the department of Yoro. Over the years, she built up a cattle farm that supported her family. But in 2023 the lagoon her herd depended on dried up, and in just 40 days she lost 15 cows. To stop relying on rain alone, she drilled a well and began to diversify, and today she raises cattle, grows chili peppers, and keeps a small apiary with her daughter. Honduras is facing a new water emergency, and producers in Yoro report a sharp drop in the milk reaching collection centers. Rural women also face barriers to credit and resources. Milexy belongs to a community savings group and shares what she has learned as a community leader and trainer.

Milexy Rodríguez, in a blue shirt and hat, and her daughter Nayeli, in white, at a cattle fair held one evening around the CREL, the community milk collection center, in a neighboring village. Organized by local ranching families, these gatherings bring neighbors together and offer a break from the daily rhythm of work on the ranch.

Rodríguez milks one of her cows on the ranch. Today she gets fewer than 10 liters a day, far below what she produced before losing her herd in the 2023 drought.

A calf feeds from its mother on Rodríguez’s ranch.

Milexy Rodríguez rides home on her motorcycle after delivering her milk to the El Edén collection center.

The project was produced with support from Heifer International.

#6651. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

#6650. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6649. Azalea Cocktail

Recipe by Kate McKiernan, Chicago, Illinois

The Azalea cocktail is the signature bright pink, lemonade-and-vodka drink of the Masters Tournament, delivering spring and summer party refreshment.

The Azalea is the signature cocktail of the Masters Tournament, and as a hostess with the mostest, I love leaning into a theme. This drink is a hole-in-one crowd pleaser, whether you’re a golf fan or not. No one can deny the lure of a pretty-in-pink, citrusy vodka cocktail like this one, a perfect sipper on a warm, breezy day on or off the green.

Named for the stunning azalea blooms that famously line the grounds of the 13th hole at the Augusta National Golf Club, the Azalea cocktail is refreshing and perfectly sweet. It’s simple on the page with only a few ingredients, but the bright acid of the lemonade and the sweet kick of the grenadine go perfectly together and work well with a neutral spirit like vodka. It’s an easy cocktail to scale up for a crowd, making it perfect for Masters watch parties, spring brunches or any gatherings that could use a little extra pink charm.

Fill a chilled rocks glass with fresh ice.

Add ice, vodka and grenadine to an empty cocktail shaker. Fill the shaker with ice, and shake the cocktail until it’s well chilled, 15 to 20 seconds.

Editor’s Tip: For a more layered look, add the grenadine directly to the glass and only shake the vodka and lemonade, allowing the pink color to settle to the bottom.

Strain the cocktail into the prepared glass.

Garnish the cocktail with an orange slice and a cocktail cherry.

Editor’s Tip: You can also use the syrup from the cherries to stand in for grenadine in a pinch.

To make Azalea cocktails for a crowd, multiply the portions by the number of people you’re serving. Combine the vodka, lemonade and grenadine in a large pitcher or beverage dispenser ahead of time, then refrigerate the mixture until you’re ready to serve. If you don’t plan to shake each drink individually, you’ll want to add water to the mixture to compensate for the dilution you get from shaking a cocktail over ice. To achieve the proper dilution, add water equal to 20% to 25% the total volume of the base mixture.

Another way to gauge: Make a single serving of your cocktail. Measure the total volume of liquid, stir the mixture with ice until it’s chilled, and measure it again. The difference is the exact amount of water you need to add per serving in your batch.

Stir the mixture well before pouring it over ice, and wait to add garnishes until serving so everything feels fresh.

A rocks glass, aka a double old-fashioned, is the traditional glassware choice for an Azalea cocktail, giving it a classic, country-club feel while keeping things simple and elegant. If you want to dress things up for brunch or spring entertaining, a highball glass also works beautifully, offering extra room for ice and garnishes.

#6647. Hidden in the Viral Last Ditch Debacle: How to Keep Lesbian Bars Alive

By September of this year, Jackie Matellian had spent months living in her truck while working several jobs to keep Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, open. She was the last remaining original founder, and the bar was in deep financial trouble. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, workers had gone unpaid, Matellian was carrying a $50,000 start-up loan, and the landlord wanted $3,900 in overdue rent.

Last Ditch had been built to do things most bars don’t even attempt. It welcomed lesbians, transsexuals, and other queer people who couldn’t afford the cover, offered a free store with food, clothing and harm-reduction supplies, and required KN95 masks or better. For immunocompromised patrons, those precautions made it possible to have a night out without gambling with their health. The bar’s radical inclusiveness was part of why people cared about it—and part of what its owners were struggling to finance it.

Desperate for cash, the bar’s management announced a policy shift with a cheery Instagram post: Saturday nights would become mask-optional. The gamble backfired. By treating accessibility as negotiable, the bar alienated immunocompromised regulars without attracting enough new customers to pay the rent. Follow-up stumbles culminated in a marathon three-and-a-half-hour community meeting that collapsed without a resolution. Rather than saving the venue, the policy pivot left Last Ditch with the worst of both worlds: fractured community trust and an unresolved financial crisis.

The drama became national entertainment, right up until October 26, when Last Ditch announced its soft closure.

The spectators moved on, but one issue remains: expecting one struggling lesbian bar to compensate for the failures of an entire social infrastructure is absurd. The irony is that Western Massachusetts built the blueprint for combating exactly this.

Women in the area have been finding ways to share the costs of lesbian social life for decades. UMass Amherst documents more than 400 lesbian and feminist groups active in the region between 1968 and 1978. Northampton had the Common Womon Club, Lesbian Gardens, Womonfyre Books, and the Nutcracker’s Suite self-defense dojo. These were places women built to make their social lives and organizing possible outside institutions that routinely excluded them.

In 1976, the women behind Common Womon pooled money to buy property through Ceres Inc., the nonprofit they’d formed, then financed renovations with help from donations and a loan. The adjacent storefront provided rental income and housed the Nutcracker’s Suite, then Womonfyre Books, so control of the property also gave the women a way to make room for other projects and help pay for the place they shared. Common Womon also collected sliding-scale membership dues, while the Valley Women’s History Collaborative lists benefits for the Common Womon Club that helped keep it going.

The womon-spelling and the names are fun to inherit; I also want us to inherit the ability to put actual premises under our control. For Last Ditch, that begins with finding out whether a new set of owners can remain in the building on terms the business can afford.

Matellian had already told the Globe she planned to turn the bar into a cooperative. For that to relieve the pressure on her, new members would need to take responsibility for work she’d been doing and agree on how the existing debt would be handled. But calling it a cooperative wouldn’t do much for Matellian if she was still the person everyone called whenever something went wrong. Sharing authority has to include sharing responsibility for the work, with limits on what any one person is expected to carry.

Sharing ownership would give people more power over decisions and occasions to disagree about them. Common Womon closed in 1982, while Womonfyre lasted until 1989. Womonfyre faced harassment and threats from outside the lesbian community as well as conflicts over sexual politics and what the shop should sell. Its archive preserves those disputes alongside bank statements and instructions for running the store.

A cooperative at Last Ditch would need procedures for making decisions in tandem with conflict resolution. Which is why I like that the Womonfyre archive makes room for instructions on running the shop alongside political disputes. A disagreement over how to run a bar doesn’t become abuse because people are arguing. Treating every conflict as a verdict on someone’s character makes it harder to agree on a change, because the argument can continue long after the conduct has stopped or the policy has been reversed.

Making that possible at Last Ditch requires paid training and a written account of all this work. A cooperative whose members can debate the mission for four hours but can’t cover a shift or pay its debt will end up crushing the same woman behind the bar.

If Last Ditch is to survive, its next incarnation must trade endless character trials for operational infrastructure: shared labor, transparent books, and creative financing strategies.

If one thing the Globe’s reporting revealed, it is that one commercial bar bearing the weight of an entire community’s social safety crushes everyone under impossible expectations. Instead, we must look for ways to anchor the politics in practical economics, share the burden, and build a room strong enough to hold the argument without tearing down the house.

Anyone asking the community to save Last Ditch needs to be prepared to share control of what survives.

#6646. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.
